**Important note:** this week is about whether a risk score used on
real defendants was fair, and who it was fair to. The arithmetic below is not
contested; it holds for any table of counts. Which fairness criterion
should matter, and who should bear the errors a score makes, are
contested, and my view is one view. A well-argued position I think is
wrong can still get full marks.

## Summary

In 2016 a newsroom reported that a risk score used in a Florida
county's courts flagged Black defendants who did not reoffend almost
twice as often as it flagged white defendants who did not reoffend.
The score's vendor, and others, replied that the score was equally
accurate for both groups: among people it flagged, the same share
reoffended, and the same score meant the same rate in both groups.
Both are correct descriptions of the same table. This week is about
why both can be true at once, and what follows.

A classifier has four rates. Two of them condition on what happened
(the false positive and false negative rates); two condition on what
the classifier said (the positive and negative predictive values).
The two sides of the dispute reported the two kinds. The three
families of statistical fairness criteria ask for one or another of
these to be equal across groups. A four-line identity ties a group's
prevalence, its predictive value and its two error rates together, so
that when two groups differ in prevalence, a classifier with the same
positive predictive value in both (neither $0$ nor $1$) has a
different false positive rate or a different false negative rate in
the two. The general version of that result, for
scores rather than flags, is stated and not proved. What remains is a
choice among criteria, and the reading's three views of equality of
opportunity say which criterion each kind of fairness supports. The
choice is a value judgment that the arithmetic narrows and does not
make.

```{r setup, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
theme_set(theme_minimal())
set.seed(313)
# cividis: viridisLite::cividis(9)[c(1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9)]
navy <- "#00204D"; slate <- "#414D6B"; cgray <- "#7C7B78"; khaki <- "#9B9477"; gold <- "#BCAF6F"; yellow <- "#FFEA46"
two <- c(navy, gold)               # the two groups, wherever there are two

# COMPAS, Broward County, Florida: the people in ProPublica's two-year file
# (compas-scores-two-years.csv, github.com/propublica/compas-analysis, 7,214 rows) whose
# race is recorded as African-American or Caucasian (6,150), counted by decile score and
# by whether they were re-arrested within two years. Counts only; no row-level data.
counts <- read.csv("../../files/compas_counts.csv") |>
  mutate(group = factor(race, levels = c("African-American", "Caucasian"),
                        labels = c("Black defendants", "white defendants")))
rates_at <- function(thr) {
  counts |>
    group_by(group) |>
    summarize(total = sum(n),           # not named n: later lines index the count column n
              p = sum(n[two_year_recid == 1]) / total,
              FPR = sum(n[decile >= thr & two_year_recid == 0]) / sum(n[two_year_recid == 0]),
              FNR = sum(n[decile <  thr & two_year_recid == 1]) / sum(n[two_year_recid == 1]),
              TPR = 1 - FNR,
              PPV = sum(n[decile >= thr & two_year_recid == 1]) / sum(n[decile >= thr]),
              NPV = sum(n[decile <  thr & two_year_recid == 0]) / sum(n[decile <  thr]),
              flagged = sum(n[decile >= thr]) / total,
              .groups = "drop") |>
    rename(n = total) |>
    mutate(threshold = thr)
}
at5 <- rates_at(5)
sweep <- bind_rows(lapply(1:10, rates_at))
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
pct1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
odds <- function(p) p / (1 - p)
```

## What you brought

Every rule that sorts people into two groups can be wrong in two
ways, and the two mistakes usually fall on different people. A fraud
flag that fires wrongly costs the person flagged; a fraud flag that
stays silent wrongly costs whoever the fraud is against. A screening
test that says "disease" to a healthy person costs that person a
course of treatment or a month of worry; a test that says "healthy" to
a sick person costs that person the treatment they needed. Keep your
own example in mind. Everything below is about what happens when the
people on one side of a rule are, on average, more or less likely than
the people on the other side to have the thing the rule is looking
for.

## The COMPAS dispute

### COMPAS

COMPAS is a risk assessment tool sold by Northpointe. From the
answers to 137 questions, none of which is race,
it produces scores on several scales; the general recidivism score is
a decile from 1 to 10, and the county that used it labeled deciles 1
to 4 "low," 5 to 7 "medium" and 8 to 10 "high." Broward County,
Florida, used the score in pretrial decisions, so a high decile could
mean waiting for trial in jail rather than at home.

In May 2016 ProPublica, a nonprofit newsroom, published "Machine Bias"
([Angwin, Larson, Mattu and Kirchner, 2016](https://www.propublica.org/article/machine-bias-risk-assessments-in-criminal-sentencing))
with a methods article beside it
([Larson, Mattu, Kirchner and Angwin, 2016](https://www.propublica.org/article/how-we-analyzed-the-compas-recidivism-algorithm)).
They had obtained the scores of more than 7,000 people assessed in
2013 and 2014 in Broward County, and they followed
each person's arrest record for two years. Their finding, in their own
sentence: Black defendants who did not reoffend were almost twice as
likely to be classified as higher risk as white defendants who did
not reoffend. And in the other direction, white defendants who did
reoffend were more often classified as low risk than Black defendants
who did.

The replies came quickly. Northpointe disputed the analysis, and a
group of criminal-justice researchers published a rejoinder; I have
not read either, and I take their content from the summary in
Chouldechova (2017), section 1, which is an optional reading this
week. Both replies made the same kind of point: the score is
calibrated (the same decile means the same rate of reoffending in
both groups) and it has the same positive predictive value in both
groups (among people flagged, the same share reoffend). ProPublica's
own methods article reports those numbers too. The dispute was never
about the table. It was about which numbers in the table a fair score
has to equalize.

**The convention for this week.** $Y = 1$ means a new arrest within two
years of the assessment, in the county's records. $\hat Y = 1$ means
the score flagged the person as higher risk, which in ProPublica's
tables means a decile of 5 or above. $A$ is race as the data record it,
"African-American" or "Caucasian"; I write Black and white. So $1$ is
the bad outcome and $1$ is the flag. The textbook's examples (hiring,
lending) run the other way, with $1$ as acceptance, and reading
someone else's coding without tripping over it is part of the skill.
Nothing in the course fixes which value of $Y$ is the good one; every
piece of material says which it is using.

### Four numbers

The table below is computed from ProPublica's published data (their
`compas-scores-two-years.csv`), restricted to the two groups, 6,150
people. I kept only counts by group, decile and outcome; nothing about
any individual is in this course's files. The rates reproduce the ones
in the methods article to the decimal.

```{r four_numbers, echo=FALSE}
at5 |>
  transmute(` ` = as.character(group), n = format(n, big.mark = ","),
            `re-arrested within 2 years` = pct1(p), flagged = pct1(flagged),
            FPR = pct1(FPR), FNR = pct1(FNR), PPV = pct1(PPV), NPV = pct1(NPV)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrrrr")
```

ProPublica's two numbers are the FPR column (of those who were not
re-arrested, `r pct(at5$FPR[1])` of Black defendants had been flagged,
against `r pct(at5$FPR[2])` of white defendants) and the FNR column
(of those who were re-arrested, `r pct(at5$FNR[2])` of white defendants
had not been flagged, against `r pct(at5$FNR[1])` of Black defendants).
The replies' numbers are the PPV column (of those flagged,
`r pct(at5$PPV[1])` and `r pct(at5$PPV[2])` were re-arrested) and the
calibration picture further down (the same decile, about the same
rate in both groups). Both sides read the same 6,150 rows.

The share re-arrested within two years was `r pct1(at5$p[1])` among
Black defendants and `r pct1(at5$p[2])` among white defendants. That
is the prevalence of $Y = 1$ in each group, the base rate, and every
result below depends on the two base rates being different. It is a
fact about arrests in one county in two years, not about anything
deeper.

### What is being predicted?

Before any rate: what is $Y$? It is an arrest for a new offense,
recorded in Broward County, within two years. What anyone cares about
is whether the person reoffended, which nobody observes. Arrest is a
proxy for it, and the gap between the two is not the same for
everyone: who gets arrested depends on who gets stopped, searched and
charged, and policing is not spread evenly across neighborhoods or
groups. There is a second gap, of the kind that arises when the
decision changes what can be observed: a defendant held in jail before
trial cannot be arrested on the street, so the outcome is observed
under conditions the score itself helped set.

Every rate in this week, the two groups' prevalences included, is a
rate of the proxy. Errors in the label move people between the rows
of the table, so they change the measured rates, and the direction
depends on how the errors line up with the score. A reoffender who is
not caught is counted as "did not reoffend," and if the score flagged
them they are counted as a false positive, so the measured false
positive rate is too high. A non-reoffender who is wrongly arrested
leaves the "did not reoffend" row, and if wrongful arrests fall mostly
on flagged people the measured false positive rate is too low. If the
errors differ between groups, so does the bias in each group's
measured prevalence and rates. I do not know the size of either gap in
these data and neither does anyone else; the point of asking is that
the base-rate difference the whole argument turns on is partly a
product of the system being evaluated.

## Rates

### The four rates and the two predictive values

A binary flag and a binary outcome give a two-by-two table of counts:

| | $\hat Y = 1$ (flagged) | $\hat Y = 0$ (not flagged) |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| $Y = 1$ (re-arrested) | true positives | false negatives |
| $Y = 0$ (not re-arrested) | false positives | true negatives |

Read across a row and you condition on the truth:

- the true positive rate, $\text{TPR} = P(\hat Y = 1 \mid Y = 1)$, and
  the false negative rate, $\text{FNR} = P(\hat Y = 0 \mid Y = 1) = 1 - \text{TPR}$;
- the false positive rate, $\text{FPR} = P(\hat Y = 1 \mid Y = 0)$, and
  the true negative rate, $\text{TNR} = 1 - \text{FPR}$.

Read down a column and you condition on the flag:

- the positive predictive value, $\text{PPV} = P(Y = 1 \mid \hat Y = 1)$;
- the negative predictive value, $\text{NPV} = P(Y = 0 \mid \hat Y = 0)$.

The textbook has these as Tables 3.1 and 3.2 (page 47), and says the
names need not be memorized. Which way each conditions does need to be
known, because the dispute turned on it. The error rates ask how the score behaved on each kind of person,
which you can only know after the two years have passed. The
predictive values ask what happened to each kind of flag, which is
what a judge who sees the flag and nothing else experiences. ProPublica
had two years of hindsight and sorted people by what happened. A judge
at a hearing has the flag. Each side reported the comparison that its
position made visible.

You have met two of these rates before under other names. A
hypothesis test that rejects a true null hypothesis with probability
$\alpha$ has a false positive rate of $\alpha$, with "null is true" in
the role of $Y = 0$ and "reject" in the role of $\hat Y = 1$; its Type
II error rate $\beta$ is a false negative rate.

### The predictive value from the rates

Within one population with prevalence $p = P(Y = 1)$, the share flagged
is, by the law of total probability,
$$
P(\hat Y = 1) = p\,(1 - \text{FNR}) + (1 - p)\,\text{FPR},
$$
the true positives plus the false positives. The positive predictive
value is the true positives' share of that:
$$
\text{PPV} = \frac{p\,(1 - \text{FNR})}{p\,(1 - \text{FNR}) + (1 - p)\,\text{FPR}}.
$$

You have seen this formula with the significance filter, as the
probability that a published finding is true: a share $p$ of the
research hypotheses tested are true (their nulls are false), tests
have level $\alpha$ and power $1 - \beta$, and the probability that a
rejection is a true discovery is $p(1-\beta) / [p(1-\beta) + (1-p)\alpha]$. Replace $\alpha$ by FPR,
$\beta$ by FNR and "true hypothesis" by "reoffended" and it is the
same computation. In both settings the quantity that nobody designing
the procedure controls is $p$, and in both it is the quantity that
decides how often a positive result is right.

The negative predictive value is the same computation on the other
column:
$$
\text{NPV} = \frac{(1 - p)\,(1 - \text{FPR})}{(1 - p)\,(1 - \text{FPR}) + p\,\text{FNR}}.
$$

## Three criteria

### Independence, separation, sufficiency

The textbook organizes the dozens of statistical fairness criteria
proposed in the literature into three families (pages 54 to 61). Each
equalizes something across the groups defined by $A$; each can be
stated for a score $R$ as a conditional independence, and for a binary
flag $\hat Y$ as an equality of rates.

| | the score $R$ | the flag $\hat Y$ | other names |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| independence | $R \perp A$ | the same share flagged in every group | demographic parity, statistical parity |
| separation | $R \perp A \mid Y$ | the same FPR and the same FNR in every group | error rate parity, equalized odds |
| sufficiency | $Y \perp A \mid R$ | the same PPV and the same NPV in every group | predictive parity, which asks for equal PPV only (a relaxation) |

Each is a property of the joint distribution of $(A, R, Y)$. When all
three variables are binary that distribution is eight numbers, and
you can check any of the criteria from those eight numbers and nothing
else. That is what the textbook means by calling them observational,
and it is where the week's title comes from.

The commitment I asked for in the lecture, which number you would want
equal as a defendant who will not reoffend, as the judge, or as the
public, has these three as its answers. The defendant who will not
reoffend is in the $Y = 0$ row and is harmed by a false positive, so
wants the false positive rate equal: separation. The judge sees only
the flag and wants a flag to mean the same thing whoever it is on:
sufficiency. The public may want the shares flagged to be equal, or
may want the misses equal; those are independence and the other half
of separation.

### The criteria on the COMPAS table

Independence fails: `r pct(at5$flagged[1])` of Black defendants were
flagged against `r pct(at5$flagged[2])` of white defendants. Separation
fails, and not only at the county's cutoff. The figure moves the
cutoff from decile 2 to decile 10 and recomputes both error rates;
the gap between the groups does not close anywhere.

```{r error_rates_by_threshold, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.8, fig.alt="Two panels. Left, the false positive rate against the threshold decile from 2 to 10, for Black defendants in navy and white defendants in gold; the navy line is above the gold at every threshold. Right, the false negative rate against the threshold; the gold line is above the navy at every threshold. A vertical dotted line marks threshold 5 in both panels."}
sweep |>
  filter(threshold >= 2) |>
  select(group, threshold, FPR, FNR) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(FPR, FNR), names_to = "rate", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(rate = factor(rate, levels = c("FPR", "FNR"),
                       labels = c("false positive rate", "false negative rate"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(threshold, value, color = group)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, linetype = "dotted", color = cgray) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ rate) +
  scale_color_manual(values = two, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "flagged if decile is at least", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Sufficiency approximately holds. The positive predictive values at the
county's cutoff are `r pct1(at5$PPV[1])` and `r pct1(at5$PPV[2])`, four
points apart; the negative predictive values are `r pct1(at5$NPV[1])`
and `r pct1(at5$NPV[2])`. And the score is roughly calibrated by group:
the observed two-year re-arrest rate rises with the decile in the same
way for both groups.

```{r calibration, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.6, fig.alt="Observed two-year re-arrest rate against COMPAS decile, 1 to 10, for Black defendants in navy and white defendants in gold, with point size showing how many people had each decile. The two lines rise together from about 20 percent at decile 1 to 70 or 80 percent at decile 10."}
counts |>
  group_by(group, decile) |>
  summarize(total = sum(n), rate = sum(n[two_year_recid == 1]) / total, .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(decile, rate, color = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(size = total)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = two, name = NULL) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 6, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "COMPAS decile", y = "re-arrested within two years",
       caption = "point size: number of people with that decile") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.caption = element_text(color = cgray))
```

The white defendants' line wobbles at the top because few of them had
high deciles (64 had decile 10, against 286 Black defendants). That is
sampling variation, and it is the one place in this week where
variance rather than bias is the issue: every rate in the tables is an
estimate from a finite group, and Chouldechova's figures show
confidence intervals that the lecture's do not.

### Calibration and calibration by group

A score $R$ with values in $[0, 1]$ is *calibrated* if
$P(Y = 1 \mid R = r) = r$ for every $r$: of the people given score
$r$, a fraction $r$ have the outcome. It is *calibrated by group* if
$P(Y = 1 \mid R = r, A = a) = r$ for every $r$ and every group $a$.
COMPAS's deciles are not probabilities, so the figure above shows the
weaker thing that is actually at stake: the same decile, the same rate
in both groups. The textbook's Fact 2 (page 61) says calibration by
group implies sufficiency, and its Proposition 1 says the converse
nearly holds: a sufficient score can be relabeled, by the map
$r \mapsto P(Y = 1 \mid R = r)$, into one that is calibrated by group.
Sufficiency and calibration by group are the same idea up to a
renaming of the score's values.

Calibration by group says less than the replies implied.

Nothing has to be imposed to get it. The optimal score,
$r(x) = E[Y \mid X = x]$, is calibrated within any group that the
features $X$ can identify (Fact 3, page 62). A model fitted well on
rich features will be approximately calibrated by group without anyone
asking for it, and the textbook shows this on census income data with
an off-the-shelf random forest (pages 62 and 63). So demanding
calibration by group is not much of a demand; it mostly certifies that
the model was fitted properly.

It is also lost when a score is turned into a flag. If $R$ is
calibrated by group and the flag is $\hat Y = 1\{R \geq t\}$, then the
positive predictive value in group $a$ is
$E[R \mid R \geq t, A = a]$, the average score above the cutoff in that
group. Two groups with different score distributions have different
averages above the same cutoff, so equal calibration does not give
equal PPV after thresholding (textbook, page 71). That is why the two
PPVs in the table differ by four points although the deciles are
roughly calibrated. It also means that "calibrated" and "predictive
parity" are two different claims; the replies made both.

Calibration checks that the score's values mean what they say. A score
that gives everyone the population's base rate is perfectly
calibrated. A score that is perfect in one group and gives the other
group its base rate is perfectly calibrated by group (textbook, page
94). Neither is a score anyone would call fair, and the second is
informative in one group only. The value judgment hidden in "it is
calibrated, so it is fair" is that a score is fair when it means what
it says, whatever it does with that meaning.

## The identity

### Derivation

Fix one group, with prevalence $p$. Its flag has some FPR, FNR and
PPV. The formula for PPV above can be read the other way round. The
odds against a flag being right are
$$
\frac{1 - \text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}} = \frac{(1 - p)\,\text{FPR}}{p\,(1 - \text{FNR})},
$$
the false positives over the true positives. Solve for FPR:
$$
\text{FPR} \;=\; \frac{p}{1 - p}\cdot\frac{1 - \text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot(1 - \text{FNR}).
$$

This is equation (2.6) of Chouldechova (2017), who introduces it with
"it is not difficult to show." It is four lines from the definition of
conditional probability and the law of total probability, and it holds
for any two-by-two table of counts whatever: it is an accounting
identity, not a model. Four quantities, one equation; fix any three
and the fourth is determined. The one that nobody designing a score
controls is $p$.

Solved for the false negative rate instead:
$$
\text{FNR} \;=\; 1 - \text{FPR}\cdot\frac{1 - p}{p}\cdot\frac{\text{PPV}}{1 - \text{PPV}}.
$$

### Unequal base rates

Take two groups $a$ and $b$ with prevalences $p_a \neq p_b$, and a flag
with the same PPV in both (predictive parity), strictly between $0$ and
$1$, and the same FNR in both. Write the identity in each group and
divide:
$$
\frac{\text{FPR}_a}{\text{FPR}_b} \;=\; \frac{p_a / (1 - p_a)}{p_b / (1 - p_b)},
$$
the ratio of the groups' odds of the outcome. If the prevalences
differ, this ratio is not $1$, so the false positive rates differ. (The
condition on the PPV is what makes the division legitimate: a flag
whose every positive is right has no false positives, one whose every
positive is wrong has no true positives, and the identity has a $0$ in
it either way.) The same argument with FNR and FPR swapped in the roles of "held
equal" and "forced apart" gives the mirror statement.

With COMPAS's two prevalences, `r pct1(at5$p[1])` and `r pct1(at5$p[2])`,
the odds are `r sprintf("%.3f", odds(at5$p[1]))` and
`r sprintf("%.3f", odds(at5$p[2]))`, and their ratio is
`r sprintf("%.2f", odds(at5$p[1]) / odds(at5$p[2]))`. So a score with
equal PPV and equal FNR in both groups would have a false positive rate
`r sprintf("%.1f", odds(at5$p[1]) / odds(at5$p[2]))` times higher among
Black defendants, at these base rates, whatever else was true of it.
The observed ratio at the county's cutoff is
`r sprintf("%.2f", at5$FPR[1] / at5$FPR[2])`; the difference from
`r sprintf("%.2f", odds(at5$p[1]) / odds(at5$p[2]))` is accounted for by
the PPVs and FNRs not being exactly equal, and you can check it by
putting all four of each group's numbers into the identity. (They
balance, as they must: the identity holds for every table.)

This is the binary-classifier version of the week's main result, and
the one you are expected to be able to derive:

> When two groups differ in prevalence, a classifier with the same
> positive predictive value in both groups, strictly between $0$ and
> $1$, has a different false positive rate or a different false
> negative rate in the two groups.

Given the two groups' arrest rates and a score with predictive parity,
some gap in the error rates had to be there; tuning the score better
at that cutoff could not have removed it. Whether the gap was
acceptable is a separate question, taken up under "Limits of the
identity" below.

### Proposition 5

The textbook states the same thing as a proposition about two of the
three criteria (page 67): if $Y$ is not independent of $A$ and the flag
has a nonzero false positive rate, separation and sufficiency cannot
both hold for the flag. One more condition is needed, $\text{FPR} < 1$:
the flag $\hat Y = 1 - Y$ has FPR $= 1$, FNR $= 1$ and PPV $=$ NPV $= 0$
in every group, so it satisfies both criteria whatever the base rates,
and the book's proof passes over it. With that condition the identity
gives a short proof. Suppose both criteria hold, so FPR, FNR, PPV and
NPV are all the same in both groups, with $0 < \text{FPR} < 1$. If also
$\text{TPR} > 0$, rearrange the identity once more:
$$
\frac{p}{1 - p} \;=\; \frac{\text{FPR}}{1 - \text{FNR}}\cdot\frac{\text{PPV}}{1 - \text{PPV}},
$$
and the right side is the same in both groups, so $p_a = p_b$, which
contradicts $Y$ depending on $A$. If $\text{TPR} = 0$, every flag is a
false positive, both PPVs are $0$, and the negative predictive values
$(1 - \text{FPR})(1 - p_a) / [(1 - \text{FPR})(1 - p_a) + p_a]$ differ
between the groups because $\text{FPR} < 1$, so sufficiency fails
anyway. That second branch is the textbook's own route.

The textbook's Propositions 2 and 3 (pages 65 and 66) do the same for
the other two pairs. Independence and sufficiency cannot both hold
when $A$ and $Y$ are dependent: if $A \perp R$ and $A \perp Y \mid R$
then $A \perp (R, Y)$, hence $A \perp Y$. Independence and separation
cannot both hold when $Y$ is binary, $A$ and $Y$ are dependent and $R$
and $Y$ are dependent; the proof writes $P(R = r \mid A = a)$ two ways
by the law of total probability and finds that the two can agree only
if $R \perp Y$ or $A \perp Y$. Both are one-paragraph arguments and
both are in the required reading. Any two of the three criteria, then,
can hold together only in degenerate cases, and the one pair where
the degenerate case is interesting (separation and sufficiency, with
perfect prediction as the escape) is the pair the COMPAS dispute was
about.

### The general result

Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2017) prove the version for
scores, not flags, and it is the one usually cited. I state it and do
not prove it; the binary case above is the version for flags. Their setting: each
person has a feature vector $\sigma$, a fraction $p_\sigma$ of the
people with that feature vector are positives, and a *risk assignment*
puts people into bins, each bin labeled with a score $v$ meant as a
probability. Two groups. Three conditions:

- **(A) calibration within groups.** In each group, of the people
  assigned to a bin with score $v$, a fraction $v$ are positives.
- **(B) balance for the negative class.** The average score given to
  the negatives is the same in both groups.
- **(C) balance for the positive class.** The average score given to
  the positives is the same in both groups.

**Theorem 1.1.** If a risk assignment satisfies (A), (B) and (C), then
either prediction is perfect (every $p_\sigma$ is $0$ or $1$) or the
two groups have equal base rates.

**Theorem 1.2.** There is a continuous function $f$ with
$f(\varepsilon) \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$ such that a risk
assignment satisfying (A), (B) and (C) to within $\varepsilon$ forces
either perfect prediction or equal base rates to within
$f(\varepsilon)$.

Theorem 1.2 is what answers the objection that exact equality never
holds in data: approximately fair on all three still forces
approximately one of the two escapes. The mapping to the textbook's
criteria: (A) is calibration by group. (B) and (C) are implied by
separation and are strictly weaker than it, because separation asks
the whole distribution of the score given $Y$ to be the same in both
groups and balance asks only for its mean. So the theorem is about a
weaker pair than Proposition 5 and still finds the same two escapes.
The authors note that in the COMPAS dispute the critics pointed at
violations of (B) and (C) and the defenders at (A) holding.

## Which fairness

### Three views of equality of opportunity

Why would anyone want one of these criteria rather than another? The
textbook's fourth chapter (pages 81 to 85) sets out three views of
what equality of opportunity means.

- The *narrow view*: treat similar people similarly, taking their
  current degree of similarity as given. Two applicants with the same
  qualifications should have the same chance. This is close to
  "individual fairness," and the book observes that it has little
  normative content beyond consistency, because it does not say what
  counts as similar.
- The *broad view*: organize society so that people of similar
  ability and ambition can achieve similar outcomes. This is not about
  any one decision; it is about schools, funding and institutions
  before the decision is reached, and it is the view associated with
  Rawls's fair equality of opportunity.
- The *middle view*: treat seemingly dissimilar people similarly when
  the causes of their dissimilarity are things we should discount, such
  as past injustice or misfortune. Decision makers have an obligation
  not to perpetuate disadvantage, and the intervention is at the
  decision, not in the institutions before it.

The book then connects these to the criteria (pages 92 to 97), with
two caveats that it states first and I repeat: every observational
criterion ignores who applied in the first place (a bank that
discourages one group from applying can satisfy all three), and
statistical criteria alone never certify that a system is fair. With
those in place:

- Calibration by group fits the narrow view. If the features are the
  relevant ones and group membership is not, calibration says the
  score does not consider the group beyond what the relevant features
  encode, and group differences in outcomes are justified by
  differences in features.
- Demographic parity relates, tenuously, to the broad view: equal
  shares at the decision as a proxy for equal outcomes in life. The
  book is careful to say the relation is loose.
- Error rate parity is, in the book's words, the hardest criterion to
  connect rigorously to any moral notion, and it is nevertheless the
  one ProPublica's finding tapped into. The book ties it to the middle
  view: if one group's higher error rate comes from historical and
  present conditions that account for differences in qualifications,
  then letting that group bear more of the mistakes perpetuates the
  disadvantage. It ties it to the narrow view as well, since one
  remedy for an error-rate gap is to collect more data and assess
  people more accurately as they are, and it concludes that error rate
  parity answers to no single principle but says something about both
  views (page 101).

The dispute over the first table is a dispute between two of these
views. The error rates are mostly a middle-view complaint; the
predictive values are a narrow-view defense. Neither is a mistake. They disagree about what a fair score
owes, and who it owes it to.

The book also says (page 97) that the two errors do not weigh the
same. A false
positive, in bail or sentencing, is an unjust denial of liberty to a
person who would not have reoffended. A false negative is a release
that turned out badly, and its cost falls on the public, and depends
on the total number of such errors rather than on how they are split
between groups. In most domains, the book says, the first kind is the
more significant as a normative matter, which is why its argument for
caring about error rates at all starts from the false positives.

### Which criterion to give up

Equal predictive value or equal error rates: the two cannot both hold.
Which would you require, and which would you give up? Who do you owe
the explanation to, and who pays for your choice: which group, and
which kind of error?

There is no house answer. A defensible position gives up predictive
parity, equalizes the false positive rate, and owes the explanation to
judges, whose flag now means something different depending on who it
is on. Another defensible position keeps predictive parity, accepts
unequal error rates, and owes the explanation to the Black defendants
who will not be re-arrested and will be flagged at nearly twice the
rate, and detained where the flag decides.
A third refuses to use a score for this decision at all, which the
textbook also lists as a response, and owes the explanation to
whoever bears the errors of the human judgment that replaces it. What
is not defensible is to treat the question as settled by the
arithmetic. The arithmetic settles that a choice has to be made.

## Cutoffs and limits

### Thresholds

A county can move the cutoff without touching the score. Move it up
and fewer people are flagged: the false positive rate falls and the false
negative rate rises, in both groups. The figure plots each group's
(FPR, TPR) pair at every cutoff.

```{r roc_by_group, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4.2, fig.alt="True positive rate against false positive rate for the two groups, Black defendants in navy and white defendants in gold, one point per cutoff from 2 to 10, joined by lines, with the cutoff written beside each point and a dotted diagonal. At the same cutoff the navy point is up and to the right of the gold one."}
sweep |>
  filter(threshold >= 2) |>
  ggplot(aes(FPR, TPR, color = group)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dotted", color = cgray) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = threshold), nudge_y = 0.04, nudge_x = 0.012, size = 3.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = two, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "false positive rate", y = "true positive rate",
       caption = "the number beside each point is the cutoff: flagged if decile is at least that") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.caption = element_text(color = cgray))
```

The same cutoff puts the two groups at different points: at the county's cutoff of 5, Black defendants are
at (`r pct(at5$FPR[1])`, `r pct(at5$TPR[1])`) and white defendants at
(`r pct(at5$FPR[2])`, `r pct(at5$TPR[2])`). There is no single cutoff
at which the two groups have the same error rates. The two curves run
close to each other, which is the textbook's "visualizing
separation" picture (pages 58 to 60): the trade-offs achievable in
both groups are the points under both curves, and coming close to the
same point in both groups means a different cutoff for each group:
decile 6 for Black defendants and decile 4 for white defendants puts
the two groups' false positive rates within a point of each other and
their false negative rates within two. That is post-processing
(textbook, pages 63 and 64): take the score as given and set
group-specific cutoffs so that one criterion holds, or nearly. Then
the same decile means different treatment depending on the group, and
the score is no longer sufficient for the flag.

The identity holds at every cutoff, in every group. Moving the cutoff
changes all three of FPR, FNR and PPV; it does not change the
constraint between them, and it does not change $p$. What a false
positive costs relative to a false negative, and the cutoff that
follows from those costs, is a different question, taken up later in
the course.

### Limits of the identity

The identity says that at these base rates an error-rate gap is what
predictive parity costs. It does not say the gap is acceptable: a
county that finds it unacceptable can give up predictive parity
instead. It does not say which criterion is right. It takes the base
rates as given, and they are rates of arrest, so the lens-A question
about who gets arrested is also a question about $p$. And it leaves
two quantities free: the cutoff, and so the costs that should set it,
and the base rate itself, which no score can change and a policy can.
The pessimistic reading, that every score can be criticized on some
fairness ground so none can be criticized on any, does not follow.
Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan end their paper (section 5) by
suggesting, for settings where one kind of error costs more than the
other, a search for scores that are calibrated and satisfy the one
balance condition for the class whose errors cost more. That is a
choice between the criteria, made in the open.

### Bias and variation

The identity is a statement about population rates, so it is about
neither bias nor variance; it is exact. Variance enters when the rates
are estimated from a group of finite size. White defendants with high
deciles are few, so the white defendants' calibration curve wobbles
at the top, and a PPV computed in a small group has a wide interval.
Chouldechova's Figure 1 shows 95 percent intervals on every bar.
When you compare two groups' rates, what tells you whether a gap is
more than sampling variation is an interval for the difference between
the two rates, not whether two separate intervals overlap.

## Lenses

What are we optimizing or predicting? Re-arrest within two years,
standing in for reoffending. Every rate in the week, the two base
rates included, is a rate of the proxy, and the difference in base
rates that the whole argument runs on is partly a fact about policing.

Which comparison gets reported? ProPublica conditioned on the truth,
two years later, and reported error rates. The replies conditioned on
the flag, as a judge does, and reported predictive values and
calibration. Each side reported the comparison that its position made
visible, and each number was correct.

Who bears the error? A false positive is a person flagged who was not
re-arrested, and detained where the flag decides the detention. A false
negative is a release that went badly, paid for by someone else. Separation failing says the two groups pay
different prices for the same score, and the identity says that at
unequal base rates a score with predictive parity has to make them.

You have to choose, so choose, and defend it. Equal predictive value
or equal error rates, not both. A vendor that ships a calibrated
score has made the choice; so has a county that adopts it; so has a
newsroom that reports error rates. A default makes the choice too,
with nobody to defend it.

What can be changed, and how? What things are considered "controlled
for" or "held fixed," and is that realistic? Every one of the criteria
takes the two groups' base rates as given. Arrests depend on policing,
and policing can be changed; the base rate is the one input to the
identity that a policy, rather than a score, controls.

And why? COMPAS is a commercial product. "Equally accurate in both
groups" is a true statement about it, and it was the statement its
vendor wanted in the headline. Who benefited from that being the
number reported, and would a more competent analyst have chosen a
different one?

## Readings

### Required

- Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan, *Fairness and Machine Learning:
  Limitations and Opportunities* (MIT Press, 2023),
  [chapter 3, Classification](https://fairmlbook.org/pdf/fairmlbook.pdf):
  "Formalizing classification" through "Varying thresholds and ROC
  curves" (pages 46 to 50 of the fairmlbook.org PDF; the four rates
  and risk scores), "Statistical non-discrimination criteria" through
  the end of "Relationships between criteria" (pages 54 to 67; the
  three criteria, calibration, Propositions 1 to 5), and "Inherent
  limitations of observational criteria" (pages 71 to 73). The printed
  edition may be paginated differently.
- The same book, chapter 4, Relative notions of fairness: "Equality of
  opportunity" with its three subsections, the narrow, broad and
  middle views (pages 81 to 85).
- A skim of chapter 3, "Groups in the population" and "No fairness
  through unawareness" (pages 52 to 54): leaving the group column out
  of a model does not stop the model from using it through other
  columns.

If time is short, the pages to keep are 54 to 67 and 81 to 85. Pages
46 to 50 are the vocabulary of true and false positive rates, risk
scores and ROC curves, and pages 71 to 73 can wait until after the
lecture.

- Larson, Mattu, Kirchner and Angwin,

  (ProPublica, 23 May 2016). The methods behind the numbers above; the

  (*8th Innovations in Theoretical Computer Science Conference*, ITCS

  <https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2017.43>): section 1 through the

- Chouldechova,
  [Fair Prediction with Disparate Impact: A Study of Bias in Recidivism Prediction Instruments](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.00056)
  (*Big Data* 5(2), 2017, 153--163,
  <https://doi.org/10.1089/big.2016.0047>): sections 1, 2.1 and 2.3.
  Equation (2.6) is the identity above; section 3, not assigned, is

- Chapter 3's case study on credit scoring (pages 67 to 71), and its
